# Lactose intolerance

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Lactose intolerance*

[Original Article Link](/library/bS0Hy2)

---

## Summary

<u>Lactose</u> intolerance is a clinical syndrome resulting from the inability to absorb <u>lactose</u> due to <u>lactase deficiency</u>. <u>Lactase deficiency</u> is caused by a genetic variant resulting in decreased <u>lactase</u> production or by disruption of the <u>epithelium</u> of the <u>small intestine</u> resulting in loss of <u>lactase</u>. After consuming food or beverages containing large quantities of <u>lactose</u>, individuals with <u>lactose</u> intolerance develop abdominal symptoms, such as <u>pain</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>, and <u>bloating</u>. <u>Lactose</u> intolerance is usually diagnosed if there is symptom resolution after a 2-week trial of a strict <u>lactose</u>-free diet. If symptoms persist, a <u>confirmatory test</u> is required (e.g., <u>hydrogen breath test</u>, <u>lactose</u> intolerance test). The condition is managed by adherence to a <u>lactose</u>-restricted diet and the use of oral <u>lactase</u> supplements.

---

## Definitions

* Lactase deficiency: low levels of <u>lactase</u> in the <u>small intestine</u> due to a genetic variant resulting in decreased <u>lactase</u> production, or disruption to the <u>epithelium</u> of the <u>small intestine</u> resulting in loss of <u>lactase</u>

* Lactose malabsorption

* <u>Lactase deficiency</u> prevents the digestion of <u>lactose</u> in the <u>small intestine</u>, leading to passage of <u>lactose</u> into the <u>large intestine</u>.

* Can be asymptomatic or cause gastrointestinal symptoms

* <u>Lactose</u> intolerance: gastrointestinal symptoms resulting from <u>lactose malabsorption</u>

---

## Epidemiology

* Approximately 70% of the world's population have a <u>lactase deficiency</u>; the <u>proportion</u> who develop <u>lactose</u> intolerance is unknown.

* <u>Lactase deficiency</u> commonly occurs in people of African, Asian, or Native American ancestry (<u>prevalence</u> is up to 100%).

* The <u>prevalence</u> of <u>lactose</u> intolerance increases with age.




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Primary lactase deficiency (lactase nonpersistence)

* Most common cause of <u>lactose</u> intolerance

* <u>Genetic polymorphism</u> in the lactase‑coding <u>gene</u> with subsequent downregulation (absence of <u>lactase</u>-persistence <u>allele</u>)

* Symptoms occur after <u>lactase</u> activity starts to decrease during childhood; the rate of decline is influenced by genetic factors.  [[2]](/library/dVYotL)

* Secondary lactase deficiency (acquired)

* Due to underlying disorders of the <u>small intestine</u> that result in <u>mucosal</u> damage, e.g.: 

* Autoimmune disorders (e.g., <u>gluten-sensitive enteropathy</u>)

* <u>Viral gastroenteritis</u> (e.g., due to <u>rotavirus</u>)

* Can occur at any age but most commonly affects <u>infants</u> [[2]](/library/dVYotL)

* Congenital lactase deficiency

* An <u>autosomal recessive</u> condition (extremely rare)

* Clinical features develop in the first few days of life.

* Developmental lactase deficiency: transient <u>lactase deficiency</u> that occurs in <u>premature infants</u>, as <u>lactase</u> activity develops late during <u>pregnancy</u>





> [!TIP]
> Not all individuals with <u>lactase deficiency</u> develop <u>lactose</u> intolerance; <u>lactose malabsorption</u> may be asymptomatic. [[1]](/library/PBWWaL0)

---

## Pathophysiology

* <u>Lactase</u> is a brush‑border enzyme that cleaves <u>lactose</u>, a <u>disaccharide</u>, into absorbable <u>monosaccharides</u> (galactose and <u>glucose</u>).

* In the case of <u>lactase deficiency</u>, an almost complete absence of <u>lactose</u> digestion is observed, resulting in decreased absorption in the <u>small intestine</u> (particularly the <u>jejunum</u>). [[3]](/library/aOaQIk)

* The transfer of osmotically active amounts of <u>lactose</u> into the <u>large intestine</u> leads to the osmotic binding of water → <u>diarrhea</u> with a high osmotic gap

* ↓ Stool <u>pH</u> (< 6): due to <u>lactose</u> fermentation by <u>colonic</u> bacterial flora

* Increased <u>peristalsis</u> due to increased intestinal filling → abdominal <u>pain</u>

* Metabolism of <u>lactose</u> via the physiological bacterial flora of the <u>colon</u>

* Formation of short‑chain <u>fatty acids</u> that exacerbate <u>diarrhea</u>

* Increased gas formation and flatulence





> [!TIP]
> <u>Lactase deficiency</u> is a <u>malabsorption</u> disorder.

---

## Clinical features

Symptoms occur about an hour to several hours following consumption of milk products; the intensity of symptoms correlates with the amount of <u>lactose</u> consumed. [[2]](/library/dVYotL)




* <u>Diarrhea</u> (often watery, bulky, and frothy)

* Cramping abdominal <u>pain</u> (often periumbilical or in the lower abdomen)

* Abdominal <u>bloating</u>, flatulence

* <u>Nausea</u>





> [!TIP]
> Symptoms vary widely as most patients have residual amounts of <u>lactase</u>.

---

## Diagnosis

There is no standardized approach to diagnostic evaluation. [[4]](/library/YBWnzn0)




### Approach [[4]](/library/YBWnzn0)[[5]](/library/VWdG4K0)




* Rule out differential diagnoses and underlying pathology.

* Assess for features of underlying causes of <u>secondary lactase deficiency</u> and workup accordingly.  [[6]](/library/bBWHzn0)

* Consider differential diagnoses of <u>lactose</u> intolerance, e.g., <u>irritable bowel syndrome</u> (<u>IBS</u>).

* Rule out <u>red flags for colorectal cancer</u> and <u>red flags in diarrhea</u>.

* Trial a 2-week strict <u>lactose</u>-free diet, taking care to exclude hidden sources of <u>lactose</u>.  [[2]](/library/dVYotL)

* If symptoms resolve, then recur with reintroduction of <u>lactose</u>: Diagnose <u>lactose</u> intolerance.

* If symptoms persist: Refer to gastroenterology to test for <u>lactose malabsorption</u>.





### <u>Lactose malabsorption</u> studies [[4]](/library/YBWnzn0)[[7]](/library/4Wd3lK0)




* The following tests detect <u>lactose malabsorption</u>; care must be taken to ensure symptoms are not attributable to a different cause.  [[1]](/library/PBWWaL0)[[8]](/library/jfd_N60)

* For children, the <u>hydrogen breath test</u> is the preferred study.

* For adults, there is no preferred test; choose based on patient characteristics, preference, and local availability. [[2]](/library/dVYotL)[[5]](/library/VWdG4K0)[[6]](/library/bBWHzn0)





#### Options




* Hydrogen breath test (least invasive)  ; [[7]](/library/4Wd3lK0)

* Principle

* Hydrogen is produced due to bacterial fermentation following the transfer of undigested <u>lactose</u> from the <u>small intestine</u> to the <u>large intestine</u>, which is then reabsorbed into the blood and excreted by the <u>lungs</u>.

* The excreted hydrogen can then be measured.

* Method

* Fast for 8–12 hours.

* Ingest 25 g <u>lactose</u> with 1 cup of water.  [[2]](/library/dVYotL)[[7]](/library/4Wd3lK0)

* Measure breath hydrogen levels at set intervals for 3 hours.

* Diagnostic result: increase in breath hydrogen levels of > 20 ppm [[7]](/library/4Wd3lK0)

* Lactose tolerance test  [[6]](/library/bBWHzn0)

* Method

* Ingestion of 50 g <u>lactose</u> [[4]](/library/YBWnzn0)

* Serial measurements of serum <u>glucose</u>   [[1]](/library/PBWWaL0)[[4]](/library/YBWnzn0)

* Diagnostic result: rise in serum <u>glucose</u> of < 20 mg/dL from pretest values [[4]](/library/YBWnzn0)

* Endoscopy with <u>small intestine biopsy</u> [[1]](/library/PBWWaL0)[[2]](/library/dVYotL)

* <u>Primary lactase deficiency</u>: normal intestinal architecture

* <u>Secondary lactase deficiency</u>: <u>mucosal</u> damage, e.g., injured tips of <u>intestinal villi</u>

* All patients: low levels of <u>lactase</u>

* <u>Genetic testing</u>: limited use in selected populations  [[4]](/library/YBWnzn0)[[5]](/library/VWdG4K0)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Food allergy</u> [[9]](/library/st0tU3)

* <u>IgE</u>-mediated: <u>cow's milk allergy</u>, peanut <u>allergy</u>

* Non-<u>IgE</u>-mediated [[10]](/library/Hy1Kgj0)

* <u>Allergy</u> to common <u>antigens</u>, such as cow's milk <u>proteins</u> (e.g., lactalbumin, casein), soy <u>proteins</u>, and egg <u>proteins</u>

* Food protein-induced <u>allergic proctocolitis</u>

* Mixed <u>IgE</u>/non-<u>IgE</u>-mediated: eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorder

* <u>Food intolerance</u>: <u>fructose intolerance</u>, intolerance of short-chain fermentable <u>carbohydrates</u>

* <u>Celiac disease</u> [[6]](/library/bBWHzn0)

* <u>Irritable bowel syndrome</u>

* <u>Inflammatory bowel disease</u>

* <u>Gastrointestinal infections</u> (e.g., <u>giardiasis</u>, bacterial or <u>viral gastroenteritis</u>)

* <u>Small bowel bacterial overgrowth</u>

* <u>Cystic fibrosis</u>

* Bowel <u>malignancy</u>




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[4]](/library/YBWnzn0)[[5]](/library/VWdG4K0)




* Advise a <u>lactose</u>-restricted diet.

* <u>Primary lactose intolerance</u>: Dietary changes will be lifelong.

* <u>Secondary lactose intolerance</u>

* Treat the underlying condition (e.g., <u>IBD</u>, <u>infectious gastroenteritis</u>).

* It may be possible to reintroduce <u>lactose</u> once the underlying condition has been managed effectively. [[1]](/library/PBWWaL0)[[6]](/library/bBWHzn0)[[11]](/library/Xu19pi0)

* Recommend ; taking commercially available oral <u>lactase</u> supplements when consuming <u>lactose</u>.  [[2]](/library/dVYotL)[[6]](/library/bBWHzn0)

* Ensure patients receive the recommended daily intake of <u>calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u> through diet or supplementation to prevent <u>osteomalacia</u>.  [[2]](/library/dVYotL)[[5]](/library/VWdG4K0)





> [!TIP]
> Although prebiotics and probiotics may reduce <u>symptoms of lactose intolerance</u>, high-quality evidence is lacking and, currently, there are no definitive recommendations. [[1]](/library/PBWWaL0)[[5]](/library/VWdG4K0)[[12]](/library/sXdtzo0)




### <u>Lactose</u>-restricted diet




* Reduce <u>lactose</u> intake. ;  [[4]](/library/YBWnzn0)

* Use lactose‑free or low-<u>lactose</u> products. [[4]](/library/YBWnzn0)

* Some <u>lactose</u> (e.g., 8–12 fluid oz of cow's milk per day) is often tolerated. [[5]](/library/VWdG4K0)[[6]](/library/bBWHzn0)

* Advise reading food labels to identify <u>lactose</u> in unexpected items (e.g., bread, certain medications, salad dressing). [[6]](/library/bBWHzn0)

* When consuming <u>lactose</u>, consume other <u>solid foods</u> to slow gastric emptying. [[2]](/library/dVYotL)





> [!TIP]
> Yogurt is usually well-tolerated because of the bacteria-derived <u>lactase</u> in live cultures. [[6]](/library/bBWHzn0)
